options.text: Only setup changes, and MCP tool definitions stay out of the context window until they are called, so context-cost checks can be dropped.
The loop stops returning `tool_result` blocks, because the MCP server sends each result straight into Claude's context after running the tool.
The loop must label MCP calls separately, with Claude treating server-provided tools as a distinct category with its own block types.
Only setup changes: the client sends `ListToolsRequest` and hands Claude the definitions; `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairing is unchanged.

questions.explanation: MCP moves tool definitions and execution into a server, but the loop is the same: Claude still issues `tool_use` blocks, the application still returns `tool_result` blocks, and the pairing rules still apply. What changes is setup, where the MCP client sends a `ListToolsRequest` and hands the returned definitions to Claude, which cannot tell them apart from authored tools. Analogy: when a cafe stops baking its own bread and buys it from a bakery, the counter, the till, and the receipt work exactly as before; only who made the bread has changed. The bakery is the MCP server and the till is your loop. The tempting near-miss forgets that connected servers still add their definitions to the context window, so context-cost checks remain necessary.

distractor_explanations.A: Connected servers add their tool definitions to the context window even when the tools go unused, so the checks still matter.
distractor_explanations.B: The application still returns each result as a `tool_result` with the matching ID; the pairing rules still apply.
distractor_explanations.C: From Claude's perspective, tools listed by an MCP server are indistinguishable from tools you authored by hand.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A security team runs an internal secrets-scanning MCP server over HTTP. It must be present for every developer in the organization, with no individual setup and no way for a developer to remove or reconfigure it. Which configuration scope fits?

options.text: User scope on each developer's machine, which applies across all of that developer's projects without touching any repo.
Enterprise scope, since an administrator deploys it through managed configuration that reaches all users and cannot be overridden.
Local scope in `~/.claude.json`, since it is stored outside the repository where developers are less likely to change it.
Project scope in a committed `.mcp.json`, since everyone who clones a repository gets the server automatically from that committed file.

questions.explanation: Scope decides who loads a server. Local scope is one project for one person, user scope is all of one person's projects, project scope travels with a repository through `.mcp.json`, and enterprise scope is pushed by an administrator through managed configuration that individuals cannot override. Analogy: a school district installs the fire-alarm system in every building; teachers do not set it up room by room and cannot unplug it, unlike the posters each teacher chooses to hang. The alarm is the enterprise-scoped server and the posters are user or project settings. Project scope is tempting because it shares automatically, but it reaches only people who clone that repository, and anyone with commit access can change the file.

distractor_explanations.A: User scope is personal: each developer would have to configure it, and could remove it again.
distractor_explanations.C: Local scope applies to one project for one person and is fully under that developer's control.
distractor_explanations.D: Project scope reaches only people who clone that repository, and anyone with commit access can edit the file.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent has `get_customer_record(id)` and `get_vendor_record(id)`. Both take a string `id`, and both descriptions read `Retrieve the record for the given ID.` On requests like `pull up record 4471`, Claude often picks the wrong tool. What does the course suggest?

options.text: Lengthen both descriptions with the history and background of each record system, so more detail separates them.
Rely on the distinct names `get_customer_record` and `get_vendor_record`, since Claude routes on names and gives very little weight to descriptions.
Add a sentence to each description naming the domain or trigger it serves, because with identical parameters routing rests on descriptions alone.
Change `id` to an integer on one tool, so the differing parameter types become the signal Claude uses to choose.

questions.explanation: When two tools accept the same parameter shape, routing collapses to the descriptions, so each one should add language naming the domain or trigger the tool is meant for. Parameter types are only a secondary signal. Analogy: two mailboxes in a lobby have the same slot and the same sign saying post here, so visitors guess, while labels reading tenants and suppliers settle it at once. The slot shape is the shared string parameter and the labels are the disambiguating sentences. Changing one slot's shape is the tempting trick, but it distorts the schema for a signal Claude weighs lightly, and longer descriptions would only bury the trigger.

distractor_explanations.A: Long descriptions bury the trigger conditions Claude reads at decision time. Specific when and when-not language separates tools.
distractor_explanations.B: Claude weighs descriptions heavily, and a request like record 4471 gives a name nothing to match against.
distractor_explanations.D: Parameter types are only a secondary signal, and the IDs may genuinely be strings. The descriptions are where the tools must differ.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is writing the description for a new `lookup_shipment(tracking_number)` tool that sits beside an existing `get_order_history(customer_id)` tool. Which TWO elements belong in the description? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Nothing beyond the tool name; a specific name such as `lookup_shipment` is enough for Claude to route on by itself.
A sentence stating that `tracking_number` is required, since the description is where required parameters are declared to Claude.
The tool's implementation history and related internal ticket numbers, so Claude has the full background on why it exists.
When to use it and when not to, for example: do not use it for a customer's past orders, which `get_order_history` covers.
An example of a valid tracking number, since the format matters and Claude must pass it in the shape the backend expects.

questions.explanation: A description should be three to four sentences covering what the tool does, when to reach for it and when not to, and what it returns, with examples of valid inputs where format matters. The when-not clause gives Claude a decision boundary against neighboring tools. Background lore buries the trigger conditions, and a name alone is not enough to disambiguate.

distractor_explanations.A: The description is what Claude relies on to decide whether a tool fits; the name alone is not sufficient.
distractor_explanations.B: Required parameters belong in the input schema's `required` array, not description prose.
distractor_explanations.C: Background lore makes the description long and buries the trigger conditions Claude reads at decision time.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team's CLAUDE.md tells Claude Code not to edit anything under `infra/prod/`. During a long session, the agent edited a file there anyway. The team wants the restriction to hold every time. What should they add?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that blocks edits under `infra/prod/`, so the restriction is enforced before the tool runs.
A second copy of the rule in the system prompt, so the restriction is stated in two places the agent reads.
A more forceful CLAUDE.md line in capital letters near the top, so the rule is harder for the agent to overlook.
A PostToolUse hook that detects edits under `infra/prod/` and asks the agent to undo each one after it has run.

questions.explanation: A rule that lives only in a prompt or CLAUDE.md is a convention; a PreToolUse hook runs before the tool call and can block it (exit code 2, or a `permissionDecision` of deny), which makes it an enforced control. PostToolUse runs after the call has completed, so it suits audit logging and formatting rather than blocking. A deny rule in settings is the other deterministic option.

distractor_explanations.B: A rule that lives only in a prompt is not enforced, however many times it is repeated.
distractor_explanations.C: An instruction is a convention the agent follows most of the time. Emphasis does not make it an enforced control.
distractor_explanations.D: PostToolUse runs after the call completes and cannot block it, so the edit has already landed.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An assistant summarizes pages from the company's internal wiki, which any employee can edit, and it can create tickets. The team argues that prompt injection is not a concern because every user of the assistant is a trusted employee. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: Injection works mainly through the system prompt, so the real risk lies in who can edit the system prompt rather than the wiki.
Injection matters when tools can send data outside the company, and an assistant that only files internal tickets has no such tool.
Internal wikis are screened by Anthropic's classifiers by default, so only pages from the public internet need to be treated as data.
The threat arrives in content the agent reads, not the user's prompt; any page someone else can edit can carry hidden instructions.

questions.explanation: Prompt injection arrives in content the agent reads, and any content someone else can write is a vector: a shared document, a database record, an email body, or a wiki page. Trusting your own users does not help, because the hostile instruction sits in retrieved content and can be indirect or hidden. The defense is to treat that content as data and constrain the actions it could trigger.

distractor_explanations.A: Injection arrives through content the model reads, such as retrieved pages, sitting in the same context as the prompt.
distractor_explanations.B: Any consequential action can be hijacked; creating tickets is an action the injected text could direct.
distractor_explanations.C: There is no internal-content exemption, and classifier defenses are probabilistic rather than guaranteed.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A bank's security reviewer asks how every action an internal Claude Code agent takes will be logged. The team's draft answer is a CLAUDE.md instruction telling the agent to append a line to an audit file after each tool call. What should the team use instead?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 after logging each call, since reviewers accept only blocking hooks as audit evidence.
A stricter CLAUDE.md instruction at the top of the file, with a reminder repeated in the system prompt for every session.
A Stop hook that asks the agent to summarize the session's actions after each turn, which then serves as the audit record.
A PostToolUse hook that logs every tool call and its parameters to an audit store, independent of what the model decides.

questions.explanation: Regulated reviewers ask where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether configuration is centrally controlled. For logging, the course's answer is a PostToolUse hook that records every tool call and its parameters to an audit store: it fires deterministically, and the log is not something the model can skip. Analogy: a shop does not ask cashiers to jot down each sale from memory; the till's receipt roll records every transaction automatically, even on the busiest day. The receipt roll is the hook's audit log and the cashier's notes are the CLAUDE.md instruction. A Stop-hook summary is tempting because it is tidy, but it is written by the model and can leave things out, so it is not a record of every call.

distractor_explanations.A: Exit code 2 blocks the call, so this would stop every action rather than record it.
distractor_explanations.B: Any instruction remains a convention the model may skip. An audit trail needs something that fires independently of the model.
distractor_explanations.C: The summary is written by the model and can leave things out, so it is not a deterministic per-call record.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A red team ran 200 injection attempts against an agent built on the newest Claude model, and the model resisted all of them. The team proposes removing the PreToolUse hook that blocks writes outside the output directory, since the model now handles injection itself. What does the course say?

options.text: Remove it, since a clean red-team run on the newest model shows its training now blocks the injections that earlier models followed.
Keep it, since training and classifiers make injections land less often but stay probabilistic, so the boundary needs enforcing.
Keep it in development but remove it in production, where Anthropic's injection classifiers screen the traffic.
Remove it but wrap retrieved content in delimiters, since tagging untrusted text as data gives the same protection as the hook.

questions.explanation: Anthropic trains models to recognize injected instructions and runs classifiers over untrusted content, which is why current models resist many attacks, but it is explicit that no agent reading untrusted content is fully immune. Those defenses are probabilistic, so the reliable boundary is what the agent is allowed to do, enforced by hooks and least privilege. Analogy: a car with excellent brakes crashes less often, yet you still wear a seatbelt, because the belt matters on the one day the brakes are not enough. Model training is the brakes and the PreToolUse hook is the seatbelt. A clean 200-attempt red-team run is the tempting evidence, but it measures how often attacks fail, not whether one will ever succeed.

distractor_explanations.A: Two hundred failed attempts show resistance, not immunity. Anthropic states that no agent reading untrusted content is fully immune.
distractor_explanations.C: Classifiers are probabilistic everywhere, and production is where untrusted content and real consequences actually meet.
distractor_explanations.D: Delimiters are a soft boundary: untrusted text can mimic them or argue to be an exception. A hook enforces the action boundary.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team records `Never modify the database schema` in `.claude/rules/db.md` with `paths: ["src/db/**"]`. While working on `src/api/helpers.ts`, the agent edits the schema anyway. What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: Rules files take effect only after `/init` regenerates CLAUDE.md to reference them; until then they are ignored.
Rules files load at launch but rank below CLAUDE.md, so an unrelated task prompt outweighs the rule; moving it to a subfolder raises its rank.
A rule applies only to files named in the task prompt, so the prompt has to list the schema files for the rule to load.
The rule loads only when Claude works with files matching its glob; a constraint that applies everywhere belongs in CLAUDE.md.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads into every session, while a rules file with a `paths` glob enters context only when Claude works with matching files. A constraint like never modifying the database schema applies everywhere, so it belongs in CLAUDE.md; path-specific guidance, such as transaction boundaries in SQL files, is what rules files are for. The agent was working outside src/db, so the scoped rule was never in its context.

distractor_explanations.A: `/init` just drafts a starter CLAUDE.md. Rules files load on their own, scoped by their `paths` field.
distractor_explanations.B: An unscoped rules file has the same priority as CLAUDE.md, and subfolders are organizational only.
distractor_explanations.C: Loading is triggered by Claude working with files that match the glob, not by file names written in the prompt.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An invoice pipeline passes an OCR wrapper's output into a prompt builder and then a Claude extraction call. The wrapper passes its unit tests and the extraction call passes its functional tests. In production, totals come back blank because the wrapper emits `amt` while the builder reads `amount`. Which test level targets this failure?

options.text: More unit tests on the OCR wrapper: a field-name bug is a defect inside one function that isolated tests are built to find.
A functional test asserting that the extraction call returns a parseable response with the expected fields for a given input.
An end-to-end test alone, since breaks that appear only in production can be caught only by running the whole flow as a user would.
An integration test that runs the wrapper's real output through the prompt builder, exercising the handoff between them.

questions.explanation: Unit tests isolate one function and functional tests check one Claude call's shape, so both sides can pass while the handoff between them is broken. An integration test exercises that seam directly, which is where the course says most silent failures hide. An end-to-end run would reveal the blank totals but is the slowest to run and the hardest to localize.

distractor_explanations.A: Each side already passes on its own. The defect lives in the handoff, which a test of one function cannot see.
distractor_explanations.B: Functional tests validate one Claude call's shape, and that call already passes. The break is upstream at the seam.
distractor_explanations.C: An end-to-end run would show blank totals but not where they came from. The seam itself is the integration level.
